This study looked at different ways to remove cataracts, which is when the eye's natural lens gets cloudy. They found that a method called phacoemulsification works better for seeing clearly after the cataract is removed. It helps people see better, but it costs more money. In some places, it costs about the same as another method called extracapsular surgery. But in poorer areas, extracapsular surgery might be cheaper.

Extracapsular surgery involves making a bigger cut in the eye to take out the cloudy part. While it doesn't cause as many problems as phacoemulsification, it doesn't help people see as well without glasses right away. Another method, called manual small incision surgery, also helps people see better but not as much as phacoemulsification.

The study found that phacoemulsification gives the best vision, but it might be too expensive for some people in poorer countries. A simpler method called manual small incision surgery can also help people see better and doesn't need special equipment. However, we still need more studies to know if this method is as good as phacoemulsification in the long run, especially about something called posterior capsular opacification, which can happen later.

Some of these studies happened in places where it's harder to get healthcare. The researchers found that giving quick treatment to a person's partner along with helping the person who has the infection (called "expedited partner therapy") worked better than just telling the infected person to find their own partner. This was true for STIs like urethritis or cervicitis. It helped keep the person who got sick from getting infected again. But when they looked at studies where many people dropped out, the difference wasn't as strong. 

The research also found that giving quick treatment to partners didn't make more partners come forward to be checked, or get treated. Sometimes, more partners were treated when the person who got sick was asked by a doctor instead of just being told to ask their own partners. However, there wasn't enough information to know which way works best for different types of STIs.

Overall, while quick partner treatment seems to work well, we don't have enough good studies to pick the very best way to do it. We need more research to figure out the best methods for different STIs.

output: This review looked at studies about whether giving antibiotics later instead of right away helps when someone has a sickness like a sore throat or ear infection. They checked if waiting to give antibiotics made a difference in how sick people felt, if they got better faster, or if their bodies had fewer problems. They found that for some sicknesses, like sore throats and ear infections, waiting to give antibiotics didn't make people feel worse or get better slower. It also helped people use fewer antibiotics overall. This means that sometimes, if a doctor thinks it's okay, they might wait to give antibiotics instead of giving them right away. This could help stop bacteria from becoming resistant to antibiotics, which is important because it makes it harder to treat infections. But it's still important to follow the doctor's advice and go back if the symptoms don't go away. The studies showed that waiting to give antibiotics wasn't different from not giving any antibiotics at all in terms of making people feel better or having fewer problems.
